title: Tools
summary: Giving a model **tools**: how a Python function becomes something a model can call, what tools return and what the model actually sees, **prebuilt toolkits** (files, web search, SQL) kept in bounds, and **the tool-calling loop** every agent runs, written by hand. The production path gives Nimbus support five tools and proves them on 12 labelled requests, including a real bug the scorecard found and how it was fixed.
learn: **@tool and args_schema**: the schema the model reads, custom names, calling tools yourself, errors and ToolRuntime
**Tool outputs**: ToolMessages, content_and_artifact, images, return_direct, reserved names
**Prebuilt toolkits**: files, DuckDuckGo search and SQL, sandboxed and read-only
**The tool loop by hand**: bind_tools, tool_calls, ToolMessages, parallel and multi-round calls
**Tool design measured**: when wording fails, change the tool
flow:
question → model.bind_tools(tools) → AIMessage.tool_calls  ──(your code runs each tool)──▶  ToolMessages
         ↑                                                                                        │
         └──────────────────────────── until the model answers without tool calls ◀──────────────┘
   return_direct tool → its output is the answer · max_rounds → stop · every call scored on 12 labelled requests

labs.explain:
A tool is a Python function plus a **schema** the model reads: `@tool` takes the name from the function, the description from the docstring and the arguments from the type hints. A Pydantic **`args_schema`** describes each argument precisely (and validates it), and you can give a tool a **custom name and description**. You can **call a tool yourself** (with an args dict, or with a ToolCall to get a ToolMessage), turn failures into messages with **ToolException + handle_tool_error**, and give a tool a hidden **ToolRuntime** argument. This lab makes no model calls: tools are plain code.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: A validated argument, and a summary for the model with the full record kept for the app.

notes.match: raise ToolException(f"No order {order_id}. Ask the customer to check the number
notes.text: A failure the model can act on: it asks the customer, instead of the conversation crashing.

labs.explain:
Whatever a tool returns, the model receives a **ToolMessage**: text, or an object serialised to JSON. **`content_and_artifact`** sends a short summary to the model and keeps the full record for your app. Tools can **return images**. **`return_direct=True`** makes the tool's output the final answer, with no extra model call. And two **reserved argument names**: `runtime` is injected and hidden; `config` must never be used (the model is told about it, but your function never gets it).

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

labs.explain:
LangChain ships ready-made tools. A **toolkit** is a bundle (pick only what you need). The lab gives a model **file tools** confined to one folder, **DuckDuckGo web search** (no API key), and **SQL tools** that explore a database and write their own queries, then checks the SQL answer against the data and shows the **limits** working: a sandbox folder and a read-only database.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

code.why: SQL tools on a read-only copy of the support orders.

notes.text: Read-only at the connection: whatever SQL the model writes, it can't change data.

labs.explain:
What every agent does, written by hand. The model sees each tool as a **name, description and JSON schema**. **`bind_tools()`** lets it *ask* for a tool (`tool_calls`), but it never runs one: your code does, appends a **ToolMessage**, and asks again, **until the reply has no tool calls**. Independent lookups come back as **parallel calls** in one turn; a call that needs another call's result takes **another round**.

After a run, **What it covers** shows each learning point with the few lines of code that do it and what they produced.

notes.text: The model now knows the tools' schemas; it still never runs them.
A ToolCall in, a ToolMessage out (with the artifact, if any).

notes.text: A return_direct tool ends the loop: its output is the answer.

path.title: Production path: Nimbus support tools
path.summary: Support gets five tools over the order system, the refund policy, the café menu, loyalty points and escalation, a hand-written tool loop with limits, and a 12-request scorecard: the right tools, with the right arguments, and a correct answer.

steps.title: The tools
steps.tagline: Five tools, written for the model
steps.explain: Support can now **look things up and act**: `get_order`, `check_refund` (the 14-day, unopened-bags policy), `cafe_menu_item`, `loyalty_points` and `escalate_to_human`. They read from a support order system (12 orders with a fixed "today", so policy answers are reproducible). Arguments are validated by Pydantic schemas, and every failure, including arguments that break the schema, comes back to the model as a message it can act on.

notes.match: def check_refund(order_id: str, opened: bool) -> str:
notes.text: Policy in code, not in the prompt: the model can't talk its way into a refund.
Bad arguments come back as "order_id: String should match pattern...", so the model can fix the call.

code.why: What the model sees when its arguments are wrong.

notes.text: The field and the rule, instead of LangChain's generic 'Tool input validation error'.

production: Tools act with your permissions: read-only by default, and every action tool (refund, pause) should go through policy checks in code, never just the prompt.
Keep tool results short: everything you return is input tokens on the next model call.

steps.title: Tool design
steps.tagline: Fix behaviour in the tool, not in the wording
steps.explain: The scorecard caught a real bug. Asked for an order's status **and** its loyalty points, the model called `get_order` and `loyalty_points` **in the same turn**, guessing the amount (₹390, ₹1,250, ₹0) instead of waiting for the order total. A clearer description ("call get_order first, never guess") **didn't fix it**. Redesigning the tool did: `loyalty_points` now takes the **order id** and looks the total up itself, so nothing has to be chained. All 12 requests now use the right tools with the right arguments.

notes.match: def points_for(order_id: str | None = None, amount_rupees: int | None = None) -> str:
notes.text: Takes what the model already has (the order id), not a value it would have to look up first.

notes.match: # scorecard the model called this in parallel with get_order and guessed the amount
notes.text: The reason, kept next to the code.

production: When a model must pass one tool's output into another, expect it to sometimes guess. Prefer tools that accept identifiers and look things up themselves.
Test dependent requests explicitly: they are where tool use breaks first.

steps.title: The loop
steps.explain: `answer_with_tools()` runs the conversation: the model asks for tools, the loop runs each one and appends the ToolMessage, and repeats until the model answers. A `return_direct` tool ends it immediately, and `max_rounds` stops a model that keeps calling tools. Module 4 replaces this hand-written loop with `create_agent`.

notes.text: A hard limit: a confused model can't loop (and spend) forever.
A tool the model invented gets an error message, not a crash.

production: Log every tool call with its arguments and result (the artifacts are perfect for this): it's the audit trail of what the assistant did.
Set max_rounds from data: these requests need 1.8 model calls on average; a request needing 5 is a problem to look at.

steps.title: Try it
steps.explain: Run any labelled request (it's scored against its label) or type your own, and see the whole conversation: what the model asked for, what each tool returned, the artifacts kept, and the answer.

steps.title: Evaluate
steps.tagline: Right tool, right arguments, right answer
steps.explain:
12 labelled requests: single lookups, refunds inside and outside the 14-day window, an opened bag, a missing order, two lookups in one message, a lookup plus points, a safety escalation, and a question no tool covers. Each is scored on **right tools**, **right arguments**, **answer correctness** (required phrases and whole numbers: 209 points must not match ₹2090), model calls, tokens and cost. The same tools **without descriptions** run as a baseline.

Measured (Mistral ministral-14b):

| toolset | success | right tools · args | tokens / request |
|---|---|---|---|
| first version | 0.83–0.92 | 0.92 · 0.96 | ~1,250 |
| **redesigned loyalty tool** | **1.00** | **1.00 · 1.00** | 1,343 |
| same, without descriptions | 1.00 | 1.00 · 1.00 | 907 |

On this set the descriptions don't change accuracy and cost 436 tokens per request. Production keeps the ones that carry rules this set doesn't test yet ("check before promising a refund", when to escalate); extending the set to cover them is the next step.
